**Observation of the test image:**

- **Plant part affected**: Base of the stem at/near the soil line; the stem has been split longitudinally to expose internal tissue
- **Visual features**:
  - White fungal/mycelial material visible at the stem base near the soil line
  - The stem is girdled/collapsed at the soil line
  - Pale, bleached stem tissue at the infection point
  - The entire plant is dead/collapsed — leaves are brown and desiccated
  - Sandy soil environment; roots appear rotted
  - The longitudinal cut reveals light-colored internal pith

**Reasoning through candidates:**

- **Southern Blight** (*Sclerotium rolfsii*): Key features are white cottony mycelial mats radiating from the stem base at the soil line, girdling of the stem at soil level, plant collapse, and small spherical sclerotia. The white fungal material at the stem base and girdling pattern match strongly.
- **Sclerotinia Timber Rot**: Also produces white cotton-like mycelium on stems and causes plant collapse, but typically infects higher on the stem and produces large black sclerotia inside; the longitudinal cut would be the diagnostic step.
- **Southern Bacterial Wilt**: Would show bacterial streaming from the cut stem, not fungal mycelium.

The image clearly shows **white mycelium at the stem base at the soil line with girdling and full plant collapse** — the hallmark of Southern Blight. No visible black sclerotia or large internal sclerotia that would confirm Sclerotinia; the infection site is right at the soil line, which is the classic Southern Blight pattern.
